# Practice a Salary Negotiation with Any AI Assistant Before the Real Talk

> **In short:** You can role-play a salary negotiation with any AI assistant — ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Copilot, or others — to rehearse your pitch, hear tough counter-arguments, and find words that actually feel like yours. The free tiers are enough for a few practice rounds, and no account trickery is required.

Salary conversations feel awkward because you only get one shot at the real thing, and the stakes are your rent. This guide shows you how to use any AI assistant as a patient, tireless rehearsal partner so you can find your words before the actual meeting. The AI can practice with you, but it can't read the room on the day — that's still you.

## Before you start
- An AI assistant account — any one works. Free plans are fine; paid plans just give you longer conversations and faster replies.
- About 15–20 minutes for the first practice round.
- A rough idea of your role, current pay, and the number you want to ask for. If you don't know the number yet, the assistant can help you estimate one in Step 2.

## Step 1 — Pick your AI rehearsal partner
Open any AI assistant you already have access to — ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Copilot, Le Chat, DeepSeek, or another — in a browser tab or its app. You're looking for the chat box, usually in the middle of the screen with a placeholder like "Message…" or "Ask anything" and a send button on the right. A free account is plenty for a few practice rounds. If you've never opened one before, the simplest path is to go to the homepage, sign in, and start typing — the chat box is the whole interface.
💬 Example: type *"Hi — I'd like to practice a salary negotiation. Can you play the hiring manager?"*
You'll know it worked when the assistant starts responding in character and asks you a question.

## Step 2 — Set the scene with a clear prompt
In the chat box, give the assistant the details it needs to play the other side: your role, years of experience, current salary, what you want to ask for, and the rough setting (a small agency, a hospital, a big tech company). Vague prompts get vague answers — the more specific you are, the sharper the rehearsal. If you don't yet know what number to ask for, ask the assistant to suggest a reasonable range first, then build the scene around that. After you hit send, the AI will respond as the manager and ask you to make your pitch.
💬 Example: *"I'm a senior graphic designer at a mid-size agency, three years in, currently earning $58,000, and I want $68,000. Please be a realistic hiring manager — push back on my number, ask why I deserve it, and don't give in easily."*
You'll know it worked when the AI responds in role and opens with something like "Okay, walk me through why you think that's the right number."

## Step 3 — Make your pitch out loud
Now it's your turn. Type — or say out loud, if the assistant has a microphone button — your opening pitch exactly the way you'd want to say it. Don't polish it first; the point is to hear how the words sound in your own voice. The AI will probably interrupt with a question or counter-argument within a sentence or two. That's the gift: in real life, pushback feels personal; here, it's just the next line of dialogue, and you can take a breath and answer.
💬 Example (your opening line): *"I want $68,000 because over the last year I've taken on the rebranding project solo, brought in two new clients through my network, and trained our junior designer. My market rate for this role in our city is $65–72."*
You'll know it worked when you get a real counter — *"That's a big jump"* or *"Where did you get that number?"* — and you can practice answering it.

## Step 4 — Handle the pushback
This is where most people freeze in real negotiations. When the AI pushes back (*"We can't go above $62,000 this year"* or *"What if we revisit in six months?"*), pause and try to answer it instead of skipping ahead. Don't accept the first "no" — force yourself to stay in character and respond. If you're stuck, ask the AI for help with a follow-up prompt. If you hate your answer, try again. The whole point of rehearsal is multiple takes without consequences.
💬 Example (your reply when the AI pushes back): *"I hear you on the budget. Could we split the difference at $65,000 now and tie the rest to clear performance goals we agree on today?"*
You'll know it worked when you've stayed in the conversation for at least three or four rounds and at least one of your answers surprised you with how steady it sounded.

## Step 5 — Try a different angle
Now restart the conversation — open a new chat, or clear the current one — and try a totally different approach. Maybe this time you lead with a competing offer, ask for non-salary perks instead (extra vacation, remote days, a signing bonus, a training budget), or try a softer opening like *"I'd love to stay, but I'm being recruited elsewhere."* Each new round gives you a different set of words to draw from on the real day. You can also flip roles and ask the AI to play you while you play the manager, so you can see what responses come up on both sides.
💬 Example: *"Let's start over. This time I'm a software engineer being offered $95,000 but I want $108,000. You be the recruiter, and please be skeptical about counter-offers."*
You'll know it worked when you've got two or three different opening lines in your back pocket that feel natural to you.

## Step 6 — Capture the phrases that felt real
Go back through the conversation and copy any sentence that made you think *"yes, I could actually say that."* Paste them into a notes app, a document, or your phone. These are your scripts for the real day — you'll likely find that you already remember most of them, but having them in writing removes one source of stress. Be honest about what felt performative, too; those lines need rewriting or cutting. Two or three solid phrases are worth more than twenty mediocre ones.
💬 Example: copy three lines like *"I'm asking for $68,000 because the work has changed, not because I've changed jobs"* into a note titled *"salary talk."*
You'll know it worked when you can close your eyes, picture the meeting, and say at least one of those lines out loud without flinching.

## Common mistakes
- **Treating the AI like a search engine.** Asking *"What's a fair salary for a designer?"* gets you a generic essay. Tell it to play a role, and the practice gets real.
- **Letting the AI be too nice.** The whole point of rehearsal is to face the awkward parts. If it folds too easily, say *"please push back harder"* and try the same scene again.
- **Practicing only the opening.** Most of the negotiation lives in the back-and-forth after your first number. Spend at least as much time on counter-arguments as on the pitch itself.
- **Skipping the "save the phrases" step.** A rehearsal you don't capture is one you have to redo. Two minutes of note-taking now saves ten minutes of fumbling later.

## What this means for you
- **In everyday life:** If a raise conversation is on your calendar, you can walk in with two or three proven opening lines and answers to the most common objections, already rehearsed in your own voice.
- **For your work:** If you hire or manage people, flip the script — ask the AI to play your employee — to rehearse a tough compensation talk from the other side, where you'll hear questions you might not have thought to ask.
- **If you're just getting started:** Pick one AI assistant, do one 15-minute practice, and write down one line that felt like you. That's the whole first move.

## Try it now
Open any AI assistant and type: *"I'm a [your job] with [X] years of experience, currently earning [$Y], and I want to ask for [$Z]. You be my manager. Push back hard."* Send it. See what comes back.
